source.title: Bigger Text Encoders Can Hurt CLIP Zero-Shot Performance
source.authors: Samir Char; Carles Domingo-Enrich; Randall Balestriero

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains and evaluates CLIP models while varying vision and text encoder sizes, testing downstream performance predictability in a multimodal setting. It does not test language-model held-out-loss power laws or compute-optimal language-model allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for its own CLIP scaling grid, downstream evaluations, loss measurements, and regression fits. Prior-work results mentioned in Related Work are not recorded. It does not fit or test a power law for held-out language-model loss, or derive a compute-optimal allocation law.
record.test_reason: The study trains a 30-model CLIP grid (vision 10M–352M, text 3M–145M) on CC3M and CC12M and measures how downstream zero-shot and linear-probe performance changes with encoder and total size. It also fits size-to-performance regressions. Its own results therefore bear on V6 (downstream performance improving predictably with scale or loss) in a new image-text contrastive setting. It fits no power law to loss and runs no compute-optimal or language-model experiment, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that CLIP zero-shot performance depends on how capacity is split between the vision and text encoders. Beyond an optimal size, larger text encoders degrade zero-shot performance through overfitting, even as total parameters grow. Modality-specific weight decay recovers and improves performance, and alignment and uniformity predict zero-shot performance. They explicitly do not derive scaling laws and present their fitted model as a description of their data.
record.recipe_differences: This is a CLIP image-text contrastive-pretraining study, not a language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling-law experiment. It varies vision and text encoder capacity independently and evaluates downstream zero-shot and linear-probe performance; it does not fit the original language-model loss laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Zero-shot outcomes depend on vision encoder size, text encoder size, pretraining dataset (CC3M versus CC12M), and modality-specific weight decay. The text-size degradation is more pronounced with smaller vision encoders; the largest vision encoder shows no degradation on CC12M. The smallest text encoder (Femto, 3M) is reported to have poor and unpredictable performance.

fits_no_version.finding: In CLIP, increasing text-encoder size monotonically lowers training contrastive loss, while oversized text encoders have higher held-out contrastive loss. Text-only weight decay improves zero-shot performance in all oversized-text configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In CLIP image-text pretraining, encoder capacity imbalance can produce modality-specific overfitting, and text-only weight decay can mitigate its downstream effects.

fits_no_version.finding: Image uniformity and alignment measured on held-out embeddings jointly predict CLIP zero-shot performance (LOOCV R2 0.810 on MSCOCO, 0.877 on Flickr30k).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For CC12M CLIP models, embedding alignment and image uniformity predict average zero-shot performance.

record.problems: Models are trained only on CC3M and CC12M, from scratch; the authors note larger datasets or pretrained initializations could change the findings. Significance tests across multiple seeds are unavailable for many analyses. Several detailed trends are presented in figures without tabulated point values. The authors state that their fitted performance model is not a definitive scaling law.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-architecture and per-task figure points from Figures 2, 3, A1, A2, A5, A6, A10, and A14 were not transcribed individually; the aggregate trends and the numerical comparisons and fits stated in text or tables were retained.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out loss and no power-law fit of loss in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs; all fits are in-sample or leave-one-out on the 30-model grid.
No fixed-compute sweep and no parameter/token allocation law. The vision–text split is a different allocation question.
Depth and width are not varied at a fixed parameter count.

CLIP is multimodal, but no power law is fitted to its loss. The held-out loss increase with oversized text encoders occurs on small datasets (CC3M, CC12M), where data is likely the bottleneck, so the V5 form is not tested.
Language models, prediction from held-out pretraining loss on the training distribution, and scales above 497M parameters or datasets beyond CC12M.
No fitted scaling exponents, no comparison of fitting choices, and no comparison of published laws.

missing.what: Zero-shot performance rises with vision-encoder size once the text encoder is adequate; the optimal vision encoder is at least 194M for every text encoder.
Linear-probe performance does not degrade with text-encoder size; it improves or saturates, and improves with the three largest vision encoders.
missing.locator: Section 4; Appendix C.4; Figs. A5, A2

missing.what: The CC3M grid shows the same peak-and-degrade pattern, and Colossal does not achieve the best performance on CC3M because of overfitting.
Spearman correlation of total parameters with zero-shot performance is r=0.62 (p<0.001); adjusted and in-sample R2 are reported for all fits.

record.verdict_notes: The CLIP setting is a different kind of system from the language models behind V1–V3, so the V6 verdicts apply only to CLIP. The headline result is non-monotone downstream performance in total parameters, which challenges a simple 'bigger is better' reading of V6. The reader's 'supports' label based on r8's R2 was removed: that fit encodes the degradation and is not a test of V6's predictability claim.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out language-model pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute.
The study does not test whether small-run language-model loss fits extrapolate to much larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation law is tested.
The study varies encoder architectures and sizes, but does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Although CLIP is multimodal, the study does not test whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.

Tests prediction of CLIP zero-shot performance from encoder size in the studied image-text setting; it does not test language-model downstream performance or prediction from language-model pretraining loss.

The study finds encoder-allocation effects and fits nonlinear performance models, but does not test language-model scaling exponents, fitting choices for those laws, or disagreements between published language-model laws.

rows.subject: CC12M CLIP architecture grid (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: 30 architectures; vision encoders 10M–352M parameters and text encoders 3M–145M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Varied text encoder size with vision encoder size held at each grid setting; evaluated average zero-shot performance over 30 tasks.
rows.measure: Zero-shot performance as text encoder size changes
rows.value: For most vision encoders, performance rises, peaks, then degrades as the text encoder grows; the degradation is more pronounced with smaller vision encoders. Colossal (352M) shows no degradation on CC12M.
rows.uncertainty: The Base–Tiny versus Base–Giant degradation is statistically significant across three seeds: one-sided paired t-test p=0.04.
rows.locator: Section 4; Figure 2(a); Appendix C.1, Table A4
rows.note: Aggregate trend stated by the authors; individual points are shown in figures. This is CLIP downstream performance, not a language-model loss law.
rows.check: Past the optimal text size, zero-shot performance falls as parameters grow for four of five vision encoders, which is the opposite of what V6 says. The rise below the optimum and Colossal's lack of degradation are the only parts that fit V6. 'Partial' understates the headline result. The same pattern also appears on CC3M (Fig. 2b), which the row omits.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, Figure 2(a); Appendix C.1, Table A4

rows.subject: Base–Nano
rows.operation_detail: Compared an asymmetric encoder-size configuration with the Base–Base reference.
rows.note: The paper reports this configuration matches or exceeds the Base–Base reference.
rows.check: 'Observed' is wrong. Base–Nano is 30.6% smaller than Base–Base yet scores 38.1% vs 37.7%, so the extra parameters give no gain. This is the authors' selected efficient configuration from the Pareto frontier, and no significance test is reported.

rows.subject: Tiny–Nano
rows.operation_detail: Compared an asymmetric encoder-size configuration with the Base–Base reference.
rows.note: The paper reports this configuration matches or exceeds the Base–Base reference.
rows.check: 'Observed' is wrong. Tiny–Nano (37.9%) matches Base–Base (37.7%) with 54.7% fewer parameters, so there is no gain from scale. It is a selected Pareto configuration with no significance test.

rows.size_stated: 30 architectures; vision encoders 10M–352M parameters and text encoders 3M–145M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Fit a saturating-ceiling regression with a capacity-mismatch penalty to predict final-epoch average zero-shot performance.
rows.measure: Leave-one-out cross-validated R2 for average zero-shot performance
rows.note: The authors describe this as an interpretable fit to these results, not a definitive scaling law.
rows.check: LOOCV R2=0.937 depends on a capacity-mismatch penalty that builds the degradation into the model. The authors call it a description, not a scaling law, and nothing is extrapolated. It shows performance is predictable from the encoder split, not that it improves with scale.

rows.subject: Base–Tiny
rows.stage_stated: Pre-trained on CC12M; three random seeds
rows.operation_detail: Compared the smaller text encoder configuration with Base–Giant across matched seeds.
rows.uncertainty: SD of paired differences 0.42; one-sided paired t-test t(2)=3.29, p=0.04; one-sided 95% CI [+0.09, ∞)
rows.note: The authors call this the smallest observed zero-shot degradation from oversized text.

relationships.condition: CLIP trained from scratch on CC12M/CC3M; text encoder scaled beyond its optimum with Atto, Tiny, Base or Giant vision encoders (zero-shot evaluation)
relationships.reason: Zero-shot performance falls as the text encoder and total size grow (r1), significantly so even in the smallest case (r9, r10). Smaller configurations match larger ones (r2, r3), and training loss keeps falling as performance drops (r16).
relationships.display_finding: Beyond the optimum, larger text encoders reduced zero-shot performance despite falling training loss, with significant deterioration even in the smallest case and smaller configurations matching larger ones.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: CLIP trained from scratch on CC12M/CC3M; text encoder scaled beyond its optimum with Atto, Tiny, Base or Giant vision encoders (zero-shot evaluation)
source_check.reason: Section 4 explicitly reports declining zero-shot performance beyond optimal text size; Table A4 confirms the Base comparison across seeds. Section 6 shows training loss nevertheless decreases.

relationships.condition: CC12M CLIP grid; predicting zero-shot performance from parameter counts
relationships.reason: Total parameters predict poorly (LOOCV R2 0.240, r4). Good prediction needs separate encoder sizes and a mismatch-penalty, non-monotone form (r5–r8, up to 0.937). Predictability depends on the capacity split, not on scale alone.
relationships.display_finding: Total parameters yielded leave-one-out R²=0.240, while modeling separate encoder sizes and their mismatch raised R² as high as 0.937.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: CC12M CLIP grid; predicting zero-shot performance from parameter counts
source_check.reason: Table A5 reports LOOCV R2 of 0.240 for total parameters and 0.937 for separate encoder sizes with a mismatch penalty. Predictability depends strongly on capacity allocation and functional form.

relationships.condition: CLIP with an adequately sized text encoder, scaling the vision encoder; Colossal vision encoder on CC12M; linear-probe evaluation
relationships.reason: Performance rises with vision size and Colossal shows no degradation (r1). Downstream performance tracks held-out contrastive loss (r15). Per the text, linear probe improves or saturates with text size (Fig. A5), which no row captures.
relationships.display_finding: On CC12M, vision scaling improved performance through Colossal with adequate text capacity; downstream scores tracked held-out contrastive loss, while text scaling improved or saturated linear-probe performance.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: CLIP with an adequately sized text encoder, scaling the vision encoder; Colossal vision encoder on CC12M; linear-probe evaluation
source_check.reason: The supporting groups exist, but the vision-scaling condition needs a CC12M restriction: Section 4 and Appendix C.4 explicitly report overfitting-related exceptions for the largest vision encoders on CC3M. Retain supports for CC12M vision scaling with adequate text capacity, Colossal on CC12M, and text scaling under linear-probe evaluation.

relation.reason: The study independently varies encoder capacities, measures downstream performance and contrastive loss, and evaluates size-to-performance predictions.

tranche.reason: The central result explicitly shows that increasing total parameters can reverse downstream gains and that scaling requires qualification by encoder allocation. This directly fits T5's results showing a version is partial or needs restating.

source_check.notes: r9 and r10 are the same paired comparison and must not count as independent evidence. Table A5 reports cross-validation within the architecture grid, not extrapolation; most other comparisons lack multiple-seed significance tests.
